rationale: A wins because it keeps the story sharp without pretending the missing facts exist. Its best line, "Klarna's AI now does the work of 700 agents — and its headcount fell 20%," is aggressive but still defensible because it immediately flags the cut-versus-unfilled hole. B has real structure, but "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" is the kind of sentence that gets a founder in trouble because the update says chats got faster, not disputes got decided by AI.
gaps_in_A: "When your BNPL dispute is decided by a chatbot" overstates the supplied facts; the update says advocates worry about AI handling disputes, not that the chatbot decides them.
"A profitable, IPO-bound Klarna leans on AI it won't fully explain" is defensible, but "leans on" needs filing-level proof before it becomes an investor-disclosure claim.
gaps_in_B: "Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes" conflates average chat resolution time with dispute resolution. That fact is not in the update.
"one of the only companies publishing operational numbers" is invented comparative context. The update gives Klarna's numbers; it does not establish rarity.
"public markets pay a premium for AI head-count reduction" overclaims both causality and market reaction before the filing/prospectus proof exists.
"let attrition cut head count 20%" misstates the facts. The update says the decline was partly through attrition and Klarna will not say how many roles were cut versus left unfilled.
